title: Phishing and Social Engineering
oneLiner: Sort a practice inbox into phishing and genuine mail, learn the red flags that give attackers away, and how the same tricks arrive by phone, text, USB stick and at the door.
keyTakeaway: Social engineering attacks people instead of systems, using urgency, authority, curiosity and helpfulness. Check the real sender and the real link target, be suspicious of any request for credentials, payment changes or secrecy, verify through a channel you already trust, and report quickly: reporting fast matters more than never being fooled.
explanation:
Phishing is a message pretending to be from someone you trust, designed to make you click a link, open an attachment, enter your password or send money. It's the most common first step in breaches, ransomware included, because it's cheap and it works: it targets people rather than software. Targeted versions aimed at one person or role are called spear phishing, and business email compromise (BEC) impersonates executives or suppliers to redirect payments, and is one of the costliest kinds of cybercrime.

Phishing messages rely on a few levers: urgency ("within 24 hours"), authority (the CEO, IT, the bank), fear ("your account will be closed"), curiosity or greed ("bonus list") and secrecy ("keep this between us"). The tells are usually in the details: a sender domain that's almost right (conperio-helpdesk instead of conperio.com, a 1 instead of an l), a link whose text differs from where it actually goes, a request to sign in through a link, and any change to bank details by email. The safe response is to verify through a separate, known channel: type the address yourself, or call the person on the number in the directory.

The same tricks arrive in other forms: vishing (voice calls from "IT" asking for an MFA code), smishing (SMS), pretexting (a convincing cover story), tailgating through badge doors, and baiting with USB sticks left in the car park. At an industrial site removable media deserves extra care; Stuxnet reached its isolated target that way. If you do click, report it immediately. Minutes matter, and a fast report lets IT reset your password, end the attacker's sessions and warn everyone else who got the same email. Sort the inbox below.
